summary: Specifies the Common Reliable Accounting for Network Element protocol, version 1.0, from XACCT. It aims to deliver large volumes of accounting data from network elements to mediation and business support systems efficiently and reliably. It is a vendor specification published as information.

plainLanguage.summary: Network gear keeps a record of who used how much, like a meter. This note describes a company's reliable way to send those meter readings to the billing computers.

questions: how does crane export accounting data reliably
how does crane handle redundant servers
why is crane better than radius for accounting
subtitle: A reliable protocol for efficiently exporting accounting data from network elements to billing systems.

tldr.problem: Existing protocols like RADIUS are inadequate for high-volume accounting data export from network elements; they are not extensible, cannot handle many outstanding requests, and do not support server-initiated messages.
tldr.mechanism: CRANE uses TCP or SCTP to reliably deliver accounting data with template negotiation to avoid redundant metadata, flow control mechanisms for reliability, and support for redundant server configurations.
tldr.outcome: CRANE efficiently exports large volumes of accounting records from network elements to mediation and billing systems with guaranteed delivery and minimal bandwidth overhead.

today: RFC 3423 is an Informational document published by XACCT Technologies. The CRANE protocol specification has been used by network equipment vendors for efficient accounting data export, particularly in carrier environments where high-volume billing records must be reliably transferred to mediation and billing systems.

sections.title: Why a New Accounting Protocol
sections.content:
Network elements must export usage information to mediation and business support systems for billing, fraud detection, and market analysis. However, existing protocols have limitations. Traditional telco export mechanisms store logs as CDR files and export them in batches; while reliable, this does not meet real-time requirements.

RADIUS is widely deployed but has fundamental constraints: it can only handle a few outstanding requests at a time, has a limited address space for commands and attributes, does not support unsolicited messages from server to client, and does not scale to high-volume accounting data.

DIAMETER retains the basic RADIUS model and eliminates several drawbacks, but its current focus is on authentication and authorization for Internet and wireless network access. Its accounting support is closely tied to authentication/authorization events, and it does not adequately address the critical issues of efficiency and performance for high-volume accounting.

SNMP-based mechanisms generally require large amounts of processing and bandwidth resources. The XACCT CRANE protocol is designed specifically to address the critical needs for efficient, reliable, and flexible delivery of high-volume accounting data from network elements.
sections.plainLanguage: Old ways of sending meter readings are slow or unreliable. New protocols were not built for this job. CRANE was designed just for exporting lots of usage records reliably and fast.

sections.title: Protocol Architecture and Design
sections.content:
The CRANE protocol runs over a reliable transport layer protocol, either TCP or SCTP. TCP meets the minimal requirements but lacks some capabilities available in SCTP, such as session-level authentication, message-based delivery (instead of stream-based), and fast connection failure detection. Therefore SCTP is the preferred transport.

The transport layer must support reliable, in-sequence message delivery; connection orientation; and fragmentation of messages up to 2^32 octets. It may support authentication and bundling of multiple messages into a single datagram.

Reliable delivery of accounting data is achieved at both the transport layer and CRANE protocol level. Transport layer acknowledgments quickly detect lost data packets and unresponsive servers, while CRANE protocol acknowledgments confirm that messages have been processed and data has been placed in persistent storage. This dual-level reliability ensures that no accounting records are lost.

A CRANE session is a logical connection between a CRANE client (running on a network element) and one or multiple CRANE servers (part of a mediation system or billing system). Multiple sessions can be maintained concurrently, distinguished by Session IDs. The CRANE protocol supports delivering accounting data to alternate CRANE servers with assigned priorities, improving robustness when one server becomes unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: CRANE runs on top of fast, reliable protocols. If the normal server breaks, it can send to a backup. The system checks in two ways that data got where it needs to go.

sections.title: Templates and Efficient Data Transfer
sections.content:
CRANE's key efficiency feature is template negotiation. Before data transfer begins, the client and servers negotiate a set of data templates that define the structure of accounting records. A template is an ordered list of keys, where each key specifies an accounting item with its data type and meaning (for example, 'Number of Sent Bytes' as an unsigned 32-bit integer).

By agreeing on templates upfront, servers understand how to interpret DATA messages without any embedded metadata. The client only sends actual accounting data values, not repeated descriptions of what each field means. This dramatically reduces bandwidth requirements.

Keys within a template can be enabled or disabled. An enabled key means the outgoing record will contain that data item; a disabled key means it will be omitted. This further reduces bandwidth by allowing servers to request only the data they need.

The complete set of templates in a CRANE client bears a Configuration ID that identifies the template version. When templates are changed, the version increments, and each data record includes both the Template ID and Configuration ID so servers can correctly interpret it.

The template negotiation process handles cases where servers have different configurations. The client publishes initial templates with TMPL DATA messages; servers can propose changes with TMPL DATA ACK responses. The client incorporates accepted changes and sends final templates with FINAL TMPL DATA messages, which servers acknowledge without further changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and servers agree on what fields are in each record once, at the start. Then the client just sends numbers, not the field names every time. The servers know what each number means because of the agreement.

sections.title: Reliable Data Delivery and Flow Control
sections.content:
CRANE ensures reliable, in-sequence delivery of accounting records using sequence numbers and acknowledgments. Each DATA message carries a Data Sequence Number (DSN). The server accepts data only when it is in-sequence and discards out-of-sequence messages.

The first DATA message after startup or after a server transition must have the DSN Synchronize bit set by the client, establishing the initial sequence number. The DSN increments by one for each new DATA message. The server MUST acknowledge reception and correct processing of DATA messages by sending DATA ACK messages containing the DSN of the last processed in-sequence message. If the server receives an out-of-sequence DATA message, it sends a DATA ACK to trigger immediate retransmission of unacknowledged records.

In a redundant server configuration, it is possible for different servers to receive different ranges of records due to server transitions. For example, one server might receive records 3042-3095 and then 3123 onward, while another receives 3096-3122. This is acceptable as long as the mediation system eventually receives all records. Each unacknowledged record is tracked, and if the amount of unacknowledged data exceeds a threshold for a configurable duration, the client should send records to an alternate server with the Duplicate bit set, suggesting the record might be a duplicate. The DSN is used by the mediation system to detect and remove duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record gets a number. The server says 'I got up to number 5042.' If the server is too slow, the client sends to a backup. The billing system removes any copies using the number.

sections.title: Sessions, Servers, and Query Messages
sections.content:
CRANE supports multiple concurrent sessions, allowing a network element to deliver accounting data to different mediation or billing systems simultaneously. Each session can consist of one or more CRANE servers in a redundant configuration. A Server Priority is assigned to each server; the client always delivers to the perceived operating server with the highest priority.

The client is responsible for configuring network addresses and priorities of all CRANE servers in a session. If the primary server becomes unreachable, the client MUST deliver to the next highest priority server that is perceived to be operating. If no perceived operating servers are available, accounting data MUST be queued in the client until a server becomes available or the queue space is exhausted.

The CRANE protocol defines three query message pairs, all initiated by a CRANE server. Get Sessions (GET SESS) lets a server query the client's session configuration. Get Templates (GET TMPL) lets a server retrieve the current template set and their enable/disable status. Status Request (STATUS REQ) lets a server request metadata about collected data, using special status templates marked with a Status bit.

All query messages include a Request ID field that the client MUST copy to the response message to match requests and responses.
sections.plainLanguage: One network element can send to multiple billing companies. Each one gets assigned a priority. If the main one breaks, it sends to the backup. Servers can ask the element what sessions it has, what records it sends, and how much data is waiting.

sections.title: CRANE Message Structure
sections.content:
Every CRANE message consists of an 8-octet header followed by variable-length payload aligned to 32-bit boundaries. The header contains:

Version (8 bits): Indicates the CRANE protocol version; Version 1.0 is indicated by setting this to 1. Version 1.0 supports IPv4 addressing but can transfer information related to IPv6 flows.

Message ID (8 bits): Identifies the message type (START, DATA, TMPL DATA, ERROR, etc., with IDs ranging from 0x01 to 0x31).

Session ID (8 bits): Associates the message with a specific CRANE session (ignored for GET SESS and GET SESS RSP messages).

Message Flags (8 bits): Identifies options associated with the message. In Version 1.0, all flags are reserved and set to zero.

Message Length (32 bits): The total length of the entire CRANE message in octets, including the header.

Messages are transmitted in network byte order from left to right. Mandatory messages that MUST be supported include START (server ready), TMPL DATA (template transmission), DATA (accounting records), DATA ACK (acknowledgment), and ERROR (error reporting). Optional messages support template negotiation, session queries, and status requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has a header saying what version, what kind of message, which session, and how big it is. Then comes the actual data.
